title: A language without "to eat"
title_target: Искам да ям — Iskam da yam
goal: Face Bulgarian's most surprising feature: there's no infinitive at all. Instead it uses **да** + a verb that still agrees with its subject — and once you're used to it, it's actually simpler.
bekal: build sentences with **искам да**, **мога да**, **трябва да**
see that the second verb still changes for the subject
express necessity with no subject using **трябва да**
accept and turn down invitations politely

dialogs.title: Диалог — Planning the weekend
dialogs.intro: Maria invites Ani on an outing. Count how many times **да** comes up, and notice that the verb after it never freezes — it always follows its subject.

lines.speaker: Мария:
lines.id: What do you want to do on Saturday?
lines.literal: what — want-you — that — do-you — on — Saturday?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: I don't know. I want to see something new.
lines.literal: not — know-I. want-I — that — see-I — something — new.

lines.speaker: Мария:
lines.id: How about going to Vitosha? The weather will be nice.
lines.literal: may — (question) — that — go-we — to — Vitosha? weather-the — will — is — nice.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: I'd love to! But I have to be back by six.
lines.literal: with — pleasure! but — must — that — myself — return-I — by — six.

lines.speaker: Мария:
lines.id: No problem. We can set off early.
lines.literal: there-isn't — problem. can-we — that — set-off-we — early.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Do I need to bring anything?

lines.speaker: Мария:
lines.id: Water and a jacket. It can get cold up there.
lines.literal: water — and — jacket. up-there — may — that — is — cold.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: OK. I love walking in the mountains.
lines.literal: fine. love-I — that — walk-I — in — mountain-the.

lines.speaker: Мария:
lines.id: Me too. So Saturday at eight in front of the hotel?

notes: **Bulgarian has no infinitive — none at all.** There's no single form meaning just "to eat", like English *to eat* or German *essen*. There are only forms that already agree with a subject. To say "I want to eat", the language says **искам да ям** — literally "I-want that I-eat". Two verbs, both changing for the subject.

⚠️ **The second verb changes too, and this is the biggest trap in this unit.** *Искам да ям* (I want to eat) but *Искаш да ядеш* (you want to eat) and *Той иска да яде* (he wants to eat). English speakers automatically freeze the second verb, because in English "to eat" never changes. Here both verbs have to match.

**Да doesn't mean "yes" here.** On its own *да* does mean "yes", but inside a sentence like this it works like "that" or English "to". Two jobs, one word — and Bulgarian ears never get confused, because the position is different.

**Трябва never changes form.** It's always *трябва*, whoever the subject is: *трябва да отида* (I have to go), *трябва да отидеш* (you have to go). The second verb carries the information about who. ⚠️ Saying *трябвам да…* is a very typical beginner's mistake.

**Може ли да… is the most common way to ask permission.** *Може ли да платя с карта?* (Can I pay by card?), *Може ли да седна?* (May I sit down?). On its own, **Може ли?** already means "may I?" or "excuse me" and can be used to call a waiter.
**Може also means "maybe, it may".** *Може да е студено* — it may be cold. Tone and context tell it apart from "may I".
**Разбрахме се literally means "we've understood each other" and it means "deal, OK".** A very common way to seal an agreement. The short form for one person: *Разбрано!* (got it, will do).
**С удоволствие — "with pleasure" — is always the right way to accept an invitation.** If you want to decline gently: *За съжаление не мога* (unfortunately I can't).

grammars.title: The да pattern — the structure that replaces the infinitive
body: The structure is always the same: the first verb agrees with the subject, then **да**, then the second verb, which agrees with the same subject.
after: To make it negative, put **не** in front of the **first** verb: *Не искам да ям* (I don't want to eat). If *не* goes after *да*, the negation moves to the second verb: *Искам да не ям* — I want not to eat. The difference is real, so watch the position.
Little words like *се, ми, го* stand **between да and the verb**: *трябва да **се** върна* (I have to get back), *искам да **ти** кажа* (I want to tell you).

grammars.title: The words most often followed by да
body: Learn these and you can build hundreds of sentences today.
after: ⚠️ **Мога is irregular**: *мога, можеш, може, можем, можете, могат*. Notice that the "I" form has **г** while the rest have **ж**. It's the most frequent verb after *съм*, so learn it now.

sections.title: Accepting, declining, and negotiating a time

head: Bulgarian
Say it
Meaning
rows: I need to think about it.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Turning down an invitation with a bare *Не* sounds sharp in Bulgaria. Always add a reason or an alternative — *За съжаление не мога, но може ли в неделя?* (Unfortunately I can't, but how about Sunday?)

sections.title: Витоша — the mountain on the capital's doorstep

blocks.text: This unit's dialogue mentions **Витоша**, and that's no random choice. Sofia is one of the few capitals in the world with a 2,290-meter mountain right at the city limits. From the center, buses and a cable car take you to stone fields and pine forests in less than an hour.

If you want one sentence to start a conversation with any Bulgarian, try: *Обичам да ходя на планина.* (I love going to the mountains.) Almost everyone here has a mountain story, and many have strong opinions about which trail is best.

blocks.title: Мартеница — the red-and-white bracelet
items: If you're in Bulgaria in March, everyone suddenly wears a little red-and-white string on their wrist or collar. It's called a **мартеница** (*MAR-teh-nee-tsa*), and people give them to each other on March 1, saying *Честита Баба Марта!*
The rule: you wear it until you see a stork or a tree in blossom, then tie it to a branch of that tree. Red stands for health and the blood of life; white for long life.
If a Bulgarian gives you one, it's a sign you've been accepted into their circle. Take it, wear it, and don't forget to tie it to a tree.

Не искам да ям. — Не мога да дойда. — Не трябва да работя днес. — Той не иска да пътува. — Не обичаме да ставаме рано.
